newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia truckers ready to launch new stoppage.
newsitem.headline: Colombia truckers ready to launch new stoppage.

text.p: The Colombian Truck Drivers' Association, which represents about 70 percent of the country's truckers, will launch a new strike to press for higher freight rates sometime in February, one of its leaders said Sunday.

The association said the threat could only be averted if President Ernesto Samper took a direct role in the matter and ordered the Transport Ministry and private transport companies to honor an agreement hammered out at the end of a crippling 11-day nationwide stoppage in October.

The deal reached in October between government ministers, transport companies and the truckers' association included an immediate 16 percent hike in freight rates, with a further increase from January 1, to take the overall increase to 30 percent.

All sides also agreed to set up a multi-party committee to look at ways of improving overall conditions for the nation's truck drivers. The group would look at issues ranging from highway tolls to vehicle licensing laws.

"We have had a small increase in freight rates, but nothing like the levels promised. None of the other conditions has been fulfilled. We have taken the decision to launch another nationwide stoppage, but have not yet set the date," Mario Quiroga, one of the association's national directorate, told Reuters.
"What we see is a trail of broken promises that shows there is a silent but unbreakable marriage between the transport companies and the government," he added.

At a meeting Saturday, the association agreed to sue the government and the transport companies, which act as middlemen between the cargo owners and the truckers, to force them to fulfill their side of the October bargain.
The association also called for a meeting with Samper, saying that the start date for a new strike will be set in February if it does not get full satisfaction.
The strike in October paralyzed key sectors of the economy, including the coffee industry.

The renewed strike call is a further blow to the embattled coffee trade. Much of the country's high-earning coffee exports is already paralyzed by a dock workers' strike at the main Pacific coast port of Buenaventura -- the shipment point for 60 percent of Colombian coffee and all sugar exports.
The stoppage began late Tuesday and is still in force. The National Coffee Growers' Federation says 160,000 60-kg bags of coffee are currently blocked in port.
Hopes of an early breakthrough were shattered Thursday when dockers rejected a deal for higher wages, which did not include additional allowances for sickness, injury and social security benefits.

In other labor news, the legal workers' union ASONAL, which represents judges and other law court staff, begins an indefinite, nationwide strike Monday. Leaders of Colombia's public sector workers and main private sector unions meet at 1700 local time/EST Monday to fix the start date for their indefinite strike, but have already said it will begin on February 4 or 11.
